The IDF says that it continues to operate at the Ali Taher Ridge and "will not allow terrorists in the area to advance and carry out" attacks on troops.
"The IDF is currently operating and will continue to act with determination against Hezbollah’s repeated attempts to harm IDF soldiers," the military adds.

events.text:
😲 One rocket system is all it takes to sink US claims of controlling Hormuz 
 
US CENTCOM recently claimed it had struck two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island capable of firing naval mines, TWZ reports—a statement that sits uneasily with the official US narrative of Iran's degraded military capabilities and loss of control over the Strait of Hormuz.
🔶 The system that Iran appears to be using is a variant of the Fajr-5 rocket—a 333mm-caliber projectile with a range of roughly 75 kilometers and a warhead capacity of 90 to 170 kilograms
🔶 It has been adapted to carry naval mines as payloads, enabling Iranian forces to lay minefields from standoff distances without risking boat crews or specialized vessels
🔶 The system can be fired from road-mobile launchers capable of shoot-and-scoot tactics, complicating US targeting efforts 
The launchers on Larak Island - an Iranian-controlled outpost in the middle of the strait—and can reach the southern shipping lanes that the US has claimed to have fully secured against Iranian attacks. Once the mines enter the water, the de-mining process can be arduous and stretch on for weeks, potentially halting all shipping through the strait.
The IRGC reported on September 2 that two tankers attempting to transit an unauthorized route in the Strait of Hormuz struck mines and were disabled—a stark reminder of this very real threat lurking in the waterway. 
👉 Admiral Brad Cooper, CENTCOM's commander, recently announced that the US had successfully cleared sea mines from the strait's international shipping lanes. President Trump has repeatedly downplayed the threat, maintaining that the waterway is "functioning" and that "the mines are gone." Yet, US officials appear to have been somewhat premature in their assessments, as the strait's already sparse traffic has dwindled to just a handful of vessels following the latest US escalation and Iranian retaliatory strikes.
The US decision to resume hostilities specifically to strike sea-mine-launching rocket systems underscores just how seriously it views this threat. Iran may have already replaced the launchers that were hit, or it may have others poised to fire at a moment's notice. While the US can clear mines, it cannot neutralize the threat of new ones being laid on short notice. Even a faint hint of such capability is enough to effectively close the strait and erode US assurances of control over the waterway.

events.text:
🇮🇱 Israel strengthens its position in Greece with a record $3.5 billion air defense deal
Israel and Greece have signed a $3.5 billion agreement that will provide Greece with a comprehensive, multi-layered air defense network, marking the largest defense export deal between the two countries and one of the biggest in Israeli history.
The deal is part of Greece's broader $32 billion military modernization plan, which also includes F-35 fighter jets from the US and frigates from France and Italy.
🔶 The "Achilles Shield" project will integrate Israeli-made systems, including David's Sling, the SPYDER and BARAK MX systems, MMR multi-mission radars, and a new national command and control system
🔶 The system will become a central element of Greece's defense architecture, rendering the country technologically and operationally dependent on Israel for maintenance, upgrades, and future development for years to come
However, questions remain about the system's effectiveness. Israeli air defense systems have already been successfully penetrated by Iranian missiles, and Greece will become dependent on a foreign supplier for technology and spare parts, which Israel, like the US in case of interceptor missiles, may decide to preserve for itself.
The defense deal is the latest step in a deepening strategic alignment between Israel, Greece, and Cyprus against [Turkey.](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73003) The countries clash for control over the Eastern Mediterranean, where rich gas deposits were discovered in contested waters. Turkey and Israel also battle [for Syria](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73592) through their proxies and compete for the position of the main power across the Middle East.
Israel's desire to draw Greece into its sphere of influence is driven by a pragmatic reality. Turkey, with 85 million people, possesses far greater manpower and military capacity compared to Israel's 9 million. As the US reduces its ability to provide support for Israel's increasingly protracted escalations against its neighbors, Israel struggles to build a new system of dependent states through economic and military leverage.

events.text:
🇮🇷💣 Cheap Iranian missiles are bleeding America's expensive Patriot stockpile dry
The night of August 30 saw one of the largest escalations between the US and Iran in recent months. US forces in Jordan fired more than 80 Patriot interceptors to counter incoming Iranian ballistic missiles, with a ratio of four interceptors per Iranian missile.
Iran designed this retaliatory attack around an interceptor-exhaustion strategy. By launching large numbers of ballistic missiles, Iran forced US batteries to fire multiple interceptors at each incoming target.
👉 Each interceptor costs $4-5 million, roughly four to five times as much as the Iranian missile it was trying to stop. In total, the operation consumed more than 10% of the entire American interceptor arsenal in a single engagement.
The Pentagon appears to have a short memory—or is too afraid of Iranian missiles to remember how empty its arsenals already are.
Patriot stockpiles were confirmed to have fallen to just 25% of the volume the Pentagon deems necessary
The shortages have forced the US to request interceptors from Poland and to suspend arms deliveries to strategic partners in Asia and Europe
👁 The Pentagon has also withdrawn THAAD and Patriot systems from South Korea to compensate for the drain
Iran can continue to apply pressure with relatively cheap missiles, while the US burns through its most expensive air defense weapons at an unsustainable rate. Meanwhile, Iran can reserve its more complex and costly missile types, such as the Fattah 2 with a hypersonic glide vehicle that is nearly impossible to intercept, for strikes on high-priority targets, guarded by almost empty launchers.
According to the Israeli paper Haaretz, 80% of Iranian missiles launched against Israeli targets have been impacting successfully. US bases in the region, already nearly defenseless, could easily follow suit.
